chapters.relation: LaRocca frames the whole volume around Kaufman's recurring 'who-what-why' of selfhood, arguing that his films literalize an inner alterity in which we are others to ourselves. He runs through Being John Malkovich (a homunculus inside another's head), Adaptation (a genetic twin), and Eternal Sunshine (memory as the very definition of who one is) to show doubling as Kaufman's method, and lists eternal recurrence among the philosophical conundra Kaufman embeds in flawed characters. The essay reads Kaufman's pseudonymity and self-naming as intensifying, not closing, the gap between the self and its double.

chapters.file: ch09 - Part 1. On Being and Not Being One’s Self.md

chapters.relation: Evans reads Adaptation as a creation story: the character Charlie Kaufman must make a script 'out of nothing' rather than transcribe Susan Orlean's Orchid Thief, so the film enacts Deleuze's idea of the writer as fabulator who confronts the audience with the text as invention. She sets Charlie's Genesis-like 'beginning without end' against Donald and Robert McKee's Aristotelian, plot-driven Story where the ending justifies the means (glossing MacIntyre's 'stories are lived before they are told'). Naming the character after himself, she argues, marks the distance between imaginative making (poesis) and Orlean's realist journalism (mimesis).

chapters.file: ch11 - On Being John Malkovich and Not Being Yourself.md
chapters.relation: Falzon argues that Being John Malkovich stages the Cartesian self as a nonbodily homunculus — Craig 'riding' behind Malkovich's eyes via the vision-limiting cutout and muffled audio — only to expose its absurdity when Malkovich enters his own portal and finds a world reduced to 'Malkovich, Malkovich.' As Craig learns to fully inhabit and puppeteer the body, the film shifts to Merleau-Ponty's and Dewey's embodied 'lived body' organized by habit. Reading Craig's takeover as Foucauldian subjectification through training, Falzon contrasts Craig's self-entrapping mastery with Lotte's genuine self-transcendence, her openness to being other than herself.

chapters.file: ch12 - The Divided Self Kaufman, Kafka, Wittgenstein, and Human Nature.md
chapters.relation: Von der Ruhr reads Human Nature through Kafka's 'A Report to an Academy,' whose humanized ape frames the film's inverted arc (Puff raised as ape, civilized by Nathan, then reverted by Lila). Using Nietzsche's herd passage and Norman Malcolm on animal thought, he argues the human–animal difference is one of kind, so Lila's Rousseauian idealization of Puff as 'uncontaminated by civilization' and Puff's claim that 'words are evil' are confused. Invoking Wittgenstein's view that art should teach and that lying presupposes truth-telling, he faults the film's bleak, self-referential loves while crediting it as a mirror of the viewer's own thinking.

chapters.file: ch13 - Unauthorized Autobiography Truth and Fact in Confessions of a Dangerous Mind.md
chapters.relation: LaRocca uses Chuck Barris's claim to be a CIA assassin to argue that autobiography makes truth rather than reports fact: unlike the earnest Confessions of Augustine and Rousseau, Barris flaunts the narrator's unreliability, and (following Stanley Fish) the autobiographer 'cannot lie' because whatever he writes is the truth about himself. Kaufman amplifies Barris's love of Carlyle's Sartor Resartus — 'the tailor, retailored' — to cast writing as patchwork quotation, contrasting Nietzsche's 'drive to truth' against literary truth. The essay closes on Clooney's literalizing adaptation, which deauthorized Kaufman, to reopen the auteur-vs-screenwriter question of who authored the film.

chapters.file: ch14 - Part 2. Being, or Trying to Be, with Others.md
ch15 - Me and You Identity, Love, and Friendship in the Films of Charlie Kaufman.md
chapters.relation: Den Uyl argues that Kaufman's films are really about friendship rather than romance, reading them through Aristotle's character friendship (the friend as 'other self' and mirror of self-knowledge) and Montaigne's ideal of a free, voluntary friendship that also engages the body. Charlie's fictional twin Donald in Adaptation externalizes the integrity Charlie lacks, and only after internalizing Donald can he say 'I love her'; Caden in Synecdoche fails because he looks only at himself. Love succeeds, on this reading, only when grounded in the self-sufficiency and self-respect that make one capable of an 'other self,' as Eternal Sunshine's Joel and Clementine haltingly discover.

chapters.file: ch16 - I Don’t Know, Just Wait Remembering Remarriage in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind.md
chapters.relation: Day reads Eternal Sunshine as Cavell's Hollywood comedy of remarriage: the kaleidoscopic middle in 'Joel's head' is the couple's remarriage conversation, a 'green world' where they invent a shared childhood and learn what it means to have memories together. Against a tape-recorder model of memory, he invokes the later Wittgenstein's private-language argument to argue there is no private memory — what Joel remembers he can return to Clementine in conversation. He rereads Mary's Nietzsche, the eternal recurrence, not as the end of regret but as affirming it (Joel's 'I wish I'd stayed. I do.'), and claims viewers themselves remember the erased past for the pair across the hallway's ten seconds of waiting.

holes.name: Stanley Cavell
holes.what: American philosopher of film, moral perfectionism, and the Hollywood comedy of remarriage, heir to Emerson and Wittgenstein.
holes.why: Chapters 15 and 16 (and the Introduction) are built on Cavell's moral perfectionism and his remarriage-comedy genre, which no existing taxonomy philosopher covers.

holes.name: The Comedy of Remarriage
holes.what: Cavell's film genre in which an estranged couple journeys back together through conversation, self-transformation, and a 'green world' retreat.
holes.why: Chapter 16 reads Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind entirely as an instance and innovation of this specific genre, which has no taxonomy concept.

holes.name: Fabulation (the writer as fabulator)
holes.what: Deleuze's notion of literature that invents rather than represents, opening onto the endless conditions of its own creation and confronting readers with the text as invention.
holes.why: Chapter 10's central claim about Adaptation — that Kaufman writes as a Deleuzian fabulator making something from nothing rather than imitating reality — has no matching taxonomy concept (rhizome does not fit).

holes.name: Auteur Theory (and film authorship)
holes.what: Truffaut/Bazin debate over whether a film's director is its preeminent author, versus screenwriter-centered 'schreiber' accounts of film authorship.
holes.why: Chapter 13 turns on the auteur-vs-screenwriter dispute (Kaufman vs Clooney) to ask who authored Confessions of a Dangerous Mind, a film-authorship concept absent from the taxonomy.
